You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Ancient societies classification

A. Sociologists and anthropologists classify societal groups according to their access to resources, prestige, and power. These factors help researchers understand how societies are organised and how authority is distributed among their members. Throughout history, scholars have generally recognised four main classifications of society. Although societies differ widely across regions and time periods, they can usually be grouped according to population size, economic organisation, and political structure. At the bottom end of the societal scale are clans, followed by tribes and chiefdoms, while states occupy the highest level. Clans are typically small and mobile, tribes are larger and often rely on farming or livestock, chiefdoms introduce ranked leadership, and states develop formal governments capable of collecting taxes, enforcing laws, and maintaining standing administrations.

B. Clans consist of small groups of people who are typically hunters or gatherers. People in a group tend to number fewer than 100 and hold no specific home, which allows for flexibility in exploiting wild food resources. Members of clans are typically related to each other through marriage or descent, and the group as a whole does not possess any formal ranks of leadership. Consequently, economic disparity between members is virtually non-existent because most individuals perform similar activities and enjoy comparable access to resources. Archaeologists believe that this form of social organisation was the dominant human lifestyle for tens of thousands of years before the emergence of agriculture approximately 12,000 years ago.

C. Today there are relatively few societal groups that fit this profile, and most have been relegated to remote regions. One well-known example is the Hadza of northern Tanzania, whose population numbers approximately 1,300 people. Researchers estimate that groups with a lifestyle similar to that of the Hadza have existed in East Africa for more than 10,000 years. Experts consider such communities particularly important because they provide valuable insight into how humans survived before farming became widespread. The Hadza continue to use many methods that resemble those employed by their distant ancestors. They hunt animals with hand-made bows and arrows and construct shelters from dried grass and branches. As was the case centuries ago, they possess very few possessions, especially when compared with their modern-day counterparts in industrialised societies.

D. Clans are also highly mobile, and their temporary homes often consist of seasonally occupied camps and other specialised sites that may be used only during certain times of the year. One feature that remains consistent is their tendency to seek out areas where large mammals can be killed and butchered. Equally important is access to locations containing suitable raw materials for making tools or carrying out other sensitive activities. Archaeological evidence from numerous continents indicates that mobile camps of this kind remained common until agriculture gradually replaced hunting and gathering as the dominant means of subsistence.

E. Tribes are generally larger than mobile hunter-gatherer clans, and it is common for such groups to include populations ranging from 2,000 to more than 10,000 people. They tend to nourish themselves primarily through cultivated plants and domesticated animals. Members of tribal societies are often farmers, although some remain nomadic, maintaining a mobile economy based on the exploitation of livestock. Tribes are usually multi-community societies whose separate settlements are integrated into the larger group through strong kinship ties. Archaeological evidence of tribal societies has been discovered in many parts of the world. Examples include the first farming communities of the Danube Valley, where agriculture appeared around 5500 BC, the Pueblos of the American Southwest, and Catalhoyuk in present-day Turkey, which dates to approximately 7500 BC. Although some tribes possess officials and even a central settlement functioning as a capital, these leaders generally lack the economic base required for the effective exercise of power.

F. Chiefs are ranked according to prestige, with senior members enjoying greater authority than others. The highest-ranking chiefs are responsible for governing society, and prestige is largely determined by how closely an individual is related to a senior chief. Despite these distinctions, there is no complete stratification into separate social classes. Chiefs often reside in centres of power and enjoy access to luxuries unavailable to most members of society, particularly temples and residences. Their privileged position is further reinforced through the receipt of surplus food and local craft products, which are paid as tribute by ordinary people. In some documented chiefdoms, households contributed several kilograms of grain or other produce annually. Chiefs could retain a portion of these resources for themselves, redistribute them among followers, or use them to support workers and specialists. Chiefdoms vary considerably in size, but populations commonly range between 5,000 and 20,000 people.

G. Statesmen share many characteristics with chiefs but differ in one crucial respect. Statesmen often possess absolute authority as kings or queens, granting them explicit power to create laws and enforce them through armed forces. The ruling lineage is generally regarded as the ultimate owner of the land, and its luxuries extend far beyond the temples enjoyed by chiefs. Such systems are sustained by lower-ranking members of society who have an obligation to pay taxes. In some ancient states, agricultural taxes could amount to approximately 10 percent of annual production. Statesmen are typically located close to capitals, where a bureaucratic administration oversees the collection of revenue and the management of key responsibilities. This centralised structure facilitates the distribution of resources to government officials, military personnel, and craft specialists. Early states developed increasingly sophisticated redistribution systems in order to support essential services and ensure the efficient functioning of government.

H. Elman Service, William Sanders, and Joseph Marino are among the scholars most closely associated with the study of social hierarchy. Service, in particular, developed an influential framework that helped organise anthropological thinking about societal development. Through a series of books and academic papers, he proposed what became known as the managerial-benefits theory. This theory hypothesises that societies organised into four levels of hierarchy and governed through centralised leadership were ultimately beneficial to their members. According to Service, leaders provided services and protections that increased in complexity as societies expanded and became more sophisticated. His research also led him to conclude that class conflict was largely absent from ancient civilisation. Rather than being compelled by force, many people willingly carried out social obligations because they believed the system benefited the wider community. Service further argued that political competition and conflict occurred primarily among members of the political elite.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Nutrition and Education

A. At the Msekeni Primary School in Malawi, children are gathered under the shade of yellow-blossomed acacia trees for their lessons. There are not enough classrooms for every class at the school, but even so, one purpose-built classroom has been emptied and turned into a storeroom for sacks of grain. Here in Malawi, it is clear that food matters more than shelter.

B. Malawi is a landlocked southern African country of great beauty and even greater poverty, and Msekeni is one of its poorer regions. Malawians are fortunate not to be experiencing the problems of war, overcrowding, or infertile ground, but still, they have trouble finding enough food to eat. Half of the children under five years of age are underfed to the point of stunting their growth. Hunger affects most aspects of Malawian life, so the country is an excellent subject for research into how nutrition and development are intertwined.

C. Bernard Kumanda is the headmaster at the Msekeni school, and he has strong views on the topic. Kumanda stated that food is essential to learning, and since 1999, his students have been receiving free school lunches of grain made up of mixed maize and soybean flour, enriched with vitamin A, which is donated through the World Food programme. Local volunteers do the cooking, turning the dry grain into a bland yet nutritious porridge to be spooned out onto plastic plates. The children eagerly line up for their share, often singing a cheerful song they call “We are getting porridge”.

D. Interestingly, the enrolment of students at the Msekeni school doubled when the school's food programme was introduced. A number of pupils transferred from other nearby schools, but most new enrolments were children whose families had previously kept them at home to work. These families were so poor that the long-term benefits of educating their children paled against the short-term gain of sending their children out to work in the fields or to gather firewood. The offer of one plate of porridge a day at school completely altered the situation. On average, when a school in Malawi starts providing free food, there is a 38% rise in the attendance of girls and 24% in boys. A child receiving food at school will not cry so plaintively for food at home. As an extra incentive, girls, who are more likely than boys to be kept at home, are even given extra snacks to take home.

E. You would expect that a school suddenly taking on significantly more students from poor homes would see a decrease in pass marks, because in most parts of the world, students from poor homes tend to perform worse than those from more prosperous backgrounds. Combining the influx of students in Msekeni with no increase in teacher numbers, you would expect the pass rates to fall even further. However, in the case of Msekeni, the opposite has proved true. Pass rates have actually improved from 30% to 85%. Although this is a particularly dramatic example of rises in pass rates, national data show that the results of school food programmes are good overall. While the pass rates for boys tend to remain the same, the rates for girls increase by 9.5%. The fact that the effect of feeding is more pronounced in girls than in boys gives a clue to who is eating first in Malawian households – it isn’t the girls.

F. Better nutrition generally means brighter children. Almost immediately, well-fed children find it easier to concentrate on their lessons – it can be well imagined what would happen to a child if his stomach is always crying out for food. “It would be easy to identify children who were critically undernourished. They were the ones who stared into space and didn’t respond when you asked them questions, ”Kumanda says. Even more importantly, though, sufficient nutritious food helps young brains grow and develop. Like all organs, the brain needs both exercise and nutrition. Lacking necessary calories, protein, and micronutrients, its growth will be stunted, just like the growth of muscles. This is why feeding children at school makes such a dramatic impact.

G. Three hundred years ago, chronic malnutrition was more or less a worldwide problem. However, now, on a global scale, people are eating better than ever before. Humans grow to around 50% larger than before the industrial revolution, and malnutrition is extremely rare in rich countries. Even in developing countries, where the majority of Earth's population lives, plates and bowls are fuller than ever before. The percentage of children under the age of five in developing countries who are malnourished fell from 39% in 1990 to 30% in 2000, according to the World Health Organization. In other places, too, the fight against hunger appears to be quite successful. Better nutrition has the effect of making people smarter and more energetic, which in turn helps them to grow more prosperous. And ironically, going from poor to well-off, people suddenly start to worry about becoming obese.

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Nutrition and Education

A. At the Msekeni Primary School in Malawi, children are gathered under the shade of yellow-blossomed acacia trees for their lessons. There are not enough classrooms for every class at the school, but even so, one purpose-built classroom has been emptied and turned into a storeroom for sacks of grain. Here in Malawi, it is clear that food matters more than shelter.

B. Malawi is a landlocked southern African country of great beauty and even greater poverty, and Msekeni is one of its poorer regions. Malawians are fortunate not to be experiencing the problems of war, overcrowding, or infertile ground, but still, they have trouble finding enough food to eat. Half of the children under five years of age are underfed to the point of stunting their growth. Hunger affects most aspects of Malawian life, so the country is an excellent subject for research into how nutrition and development are intertwined.

C. Bernard Kumanda is the headmaster at the Msekeni school, and he has strong views on the topic. Kumanda stated that food is essential to learning, and since 1999, his students have been receiving free school lunches of grain made up of mixed maize and soybean flour, enriched with vitamin A, which is donated through the World Food programme. Local volunteers do the cooking, turning the dry grain into a bland yet nutritious porridge to be spooned out onto plastic plates. The children eagerly line up for their share, often singing a cheerful song they call “We are getting porridge”.

D. Interestingly, the enrolment of students at the Msekeni school doubled when the school's food programme was introduced. A number of pupils transferred from other nearby schools, but most new enrolments were children whose families had previously kept them at home to work. These families were so poor that the long-term benefits of educating their children paled against the short-term gain of sending their children out to work in the fields or to gather firewood. The offer of one plate of porridge a day at school completely altered the situation. On average, when a school in Malawi starts providing free food, there is a 38% rise in the attendance of girls and 24% in boys. A child receiving food at school will not cry so plaintively for food at home. As an extra incentive, girls, who are more likely than boys to be kept at home, are even given extra snacks to take home.

E. You would expect that a school suddenly taking on significantly more students from poor homes would see a decrease in pass marks, because in most parts of the world, students from poor homes tend to perform worse than those from more prosperous backgrounds. Combining the influx of students in Msekeni with no increase in teacher numbers, you would expect the pass rates to fall even further. However, in the case of Msekeni, the opposite has proved true. Pass rates have actually improved from 30% to 85%. Although this is a particularly dramatic example of rises in pass rates, national data show that the results of school food programmes are good overall. While the pass rates for boys tend to remain the same, the rates for girls increase by 9.5%. The fact that the effect of feeding is more pronounced in girls than in boys gives a clue to who is eating first in Malawian households – it isn’t the girls.

F. Better nutrition generally means brighter children. Almost immediately, well-fed children find it easier to concentrate on their lessons – it can be well imagined what would happen to a child if his stomach is always crying out for food. “It would be easy to identify children who were critically undernourished. They were the ones who stared into space and didn’t respond when you asked them questions, ”Kumanda says. Even more importantly, though, sufficient nutritious food helps young brains grow and develop. Like all organs, the brain needs both exercise and nutrition. Lacking necessary calories, protein, and micronutrients, its growth will be stunted, just like the growth of muscles. This is why feeding children at school makes such a dramatic impact.

G. Three hundred years ago, chronic malnutrition was more or less a worldwide problem. However, now, on a global scale, people are eating better than ever before. Humans grow to around 50% larger than before the industrial revolution, and malnutrition is extremely rare in rich countries. Even in developing countries, where the majority of Earth's population lives, plates and bowls are fuller than ever before. The percentage of children under the age of five in developing countries who are malnourished fell from 39% in 1990 to 30% in 2000, according to the World Health Organization. In other places, too, the fight against hunger appears to be quite successful. Better nutrition has the effect of making people smarter and more energetic, which in turn helps them to grow more prosperous. And ironically, going from poor to well-off, people suddenly start to worry about becoming obese.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

Marketing and The Information Age

A. For the early practitioners of marketing in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the business of selling was simply a matter of continually finding new customers. By contrast, marketing managers in the current era recognise the importance of gathering information about the market and about potential customers. They recognise that if companies are to be profitable, customers must gain and retain their perceptions of value from the brands they buy over a long time frame, rather than from a single transaction. This also means that customers must see value in returning continually to the stores where they shop, as well as to the service providers they deal with.

B. Marketing practitioners and marketing scientists have never worked more closely than they currently do. There are many reasons for this, including the fact that this is the information age where convergence in telecommunications, media and technology is causing old ways to be challenged, and new methods and tools to be tested. Customer expectations have risen as new technologies allow new approaches. For instance, the subscriber-TV music channel Channel V encourages its viewers to sign up for text messages and email alerts that tell them when their favourite artists and songs are about to be broadcast. Competitive advantage lies in being able to recognise which customers can be given greater attention, not just because they demand it but because it makes commercial sense to provide high levels of product quality and service.

C. Modern marketing information systems rely on information technology to enable marketing intelligence to be gathered and to store and analyse marketing research information. While some of the information used is gathered by government bodies such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics and Statistics New Zealand, most of it is purposefully gathered by marketing organisations for client companies. In the process, computer technology is used to manipulate the data and then to present the information in such a way that executives can readily identify any problems or issues, and quickly arrive at solutions.

D. In order to produce superior value and satisfaction for customers, marketing managers need information at almost every turn. They need information about customers – end-users and resellers – as well as competitors and governmental and other forces in the marketplace. One marketing executive put it this way: ‘To manage a business well is to manage its future; and to manage the future is to manage information.’ Increasingly, marketers are viewing information not just as an input for making better decisions but also as an important strategic asset and marketing tool. As household incomes increase, choice widens and buyers become better at discriminating, so sellers need information about how buyers respond to different products and advertising campaigns.

E. The supply of information has also increased greatly. It has been suggested by the futurist and best-selling author John Naisbitt that the United States and, by observation, developed countries such as Australia, New Zealand and Singapore are moving from industrial to information-based economies. These post-industrial economies earn 70–80% of their Gross Domestic Product from services, and have entered what some commentators have termed the ‘Information Age’ or the ‘Information Technology Era’.

F. One study found that with all the information now available through supermarket scanners, a packaged-goods product controller is bombarded with one million to one billion new numbers each week. As Naisbitt points out: ‘Running out of information is not a problem, but drowning in it is.’ Yet marketers frequently complain that they lack information of the right kind but have plenty of the wrong kind, or they claim that marketing information is so widely spread throughout the organisation that it takes great effort to locate even simple facts. In addition, subordinates may withhold information they believe will reflect badly on their performance and important information often arrives too late to be useful, or on-time information is not accurate. So marketing managers need better information. Although marketing organisations have greater capacity to provide managers with information, they often do not use it well. As a result, many marketing organisations are now studying their managers’ information needs and designing information systems specifically to meet those needs.

G. One solution is to use a Marketing Information System (MIS). This consists of people, equipment, and procedures which, when put together, are able to gather, analyse, evaluate and distribute needed, timely, and accurate information to marketing decision-makers. The MIS begins and ends with marketing managers. First, it interacts with these managers to assess the information needs they have. Next, it develops the needed information from internal records, marketing intelligence activities, and the research process. The analysis unit processes the data to make it more useful, and finally, the MIS distributes it to managers in the right form and at the right time to help them make better marketing decisions.

H. However, the costs of obtaining, processing, storing and delivering information can mount quickly. In some cases, additional information will do little to change or improve a manager’s decision, or the costs of the information will exceed the returns from the improved decision. For example, if an organisation estimates that launching a new product without any further information will yield a profit of $500,000, then it would be foolish to spend $30,000 for additional information that would increase the profit to only $525,000. By itself, information is valueless – its value comes from its use.
